$$

$$

For example, suppose we want to evaluate the triple integral

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R x^2 + y^2 \:\textrm{d}V
$$

where $R$ is the finite region enclosed between the surfaces $z =0$ and $z = 1 - x^2 - y^2,$ as shown below.

![](images/a6/a63e349d2776fe07077379b9d603e32ad2ff264cfa8005a226422b44f7e100fe.png)

 

This is a challenging integral to evaluate as it currently stands. However, we should recognize that the problem naturally lends itself to cylindrical polar coordinates.

Recall that if $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad
y = r\sin\theta, \qquad 
z = z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](images/b2/b2f8a6fe7f21b062eec294522e411c1e471b564eae68763d4767f917d65b54b0.png)

Notice that the region $R$ is

- bounded below by $z = 0,$ and

- bounded above by $z = 1 - x^2 - y^2 = 1 - r^2.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi, \: 0 \leq z \leq 1-r^2 \right\}.
$$

![](images/da/dae76df462a695e655ffdde01559d19bf245aa6d601100fb8c7bc1024106a4c8.png)

 

To express our integral in terms of cylindrical polar coordinates, we will use the change of variables formula, given by

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, {\color{blue}\mathrm{d}V} = 
\iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \:  {\color{blue}r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta}.
$$

When expressing our integral in cylindrical polar coordinates, we must write 

$$
{\color{blue}{\textrm{d}V}} = {\color{blue}r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta}.
$$

It's important not to forget the extra factor of ${\color{blue}{r}}.$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{r}^{2}}{r}^{3}\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating this integral using the usual methods, we get

$$
\int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,white]{\color{black}1}} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,white]{\color{black}1 - r^2 }} \bbox[2pt,white]{\color{black} r^3} \: \mathrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta
=
\dfrac{\pi}{6}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R x^2 + y^2 \:\textrm{d}V = \dfrac{\pi}{6}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130470 :tutorial/content "Let's now build some intuition behind the meaning of the volume element $\textrm d V.$ This will help us to understand the change of variables formula in cylindrical polar coordinates. Suppose we have a point $P$ and a neighboring point $Q$ in the Cartesian $xyz$-space, as shown below. 

![](images/25/2535744585beb7fed89d760c0290a04f54d0a08c8f7e564b17c8e42432da031e.png)

 

Imagine moving from $P$ to $Q$ as follows:

- First, we move a distance $\textrm d x$ parallel to the $x$-axis so that the new point $P'$ has the same $x$-coordinate as $Q.$

- Then, we move a distance $\textrm d y$ parallel to the $y$-axis so that the new point $P''$ has the same $y$-coordinate as $Q.$

- Finally, we move a distance $\textrm d z$ parallel to the $z$-axis to land to $Q.$

These movements span the rectangular solid shown above. The volume of this solid, denoted $\textrm d V,$ is given by

$$
\mathrm{d}V = \mathrm{d}x \, \mathrm{d}y \, \mathrm{d}z.
$$

Thus, the element $\textrm d V$ represents the volume generated by moving from the point $P$ to the point $Q$ in this coordinate system." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130473 :tutorial/content "Let's now repeat this process for a cylindrical polar system. ![](images/24/243d720546357a33eac3f96b84755cf6aeebafdef3a3672a3d29989147f134c2.png)

- Then, we sweep through an angle $\textrm d \theta$ so that the new point $P''$ has the same $\theta$-coordinate as $Q.$ The arc length traced out by this movement approximately equals $r\,\textrm d \theta.$

- Finally, we move a distance $\textrm d z$ vertically to land on $Q.$

$$

For example, suppose we want to evaluate the triple integral

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R x^2 + y^2 \:\textrm{d}V
$$

where $R$ is the finite region enclosed between the surfaces $z =0$ and $z = 1 - x^2 - y^2,$ as shown below.

![](images/a6/a63e349d2776fe07077379b9d603e32ad2ff264cfa8005a226422b44f7e100fe.png)

 

This is a challenging integral to evaluate as it currently stands. However, we should recognize that the problem naturally lends itself to cylindrical polar coordinates.

Recall that if $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad
y = r\sin\theta, \qquad 
z = z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](images/b2/b2f8a6fe7f21b062eec294522e411c1e471b564eae68763d4767f917d65b54b0.png)

Notice that the region $R$ is

- bounded below by $z = 0,$ and

- bounded above by $z = 1 - x^2 - y^2 = 1 - r^2.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi, \: 0 \leq z \leq 1-r^2 \right\}.
$$

![](images/da/dae76df462a695e655ffdde01559d19bf245aa6d601100fb8c7bc1024106a4c8.png)

 

To express our integral in terms of cylindrical polar coordinates, we will use the change of variables formula, given by

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, {\color{blue}\mathrm{d}V} = 
\iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \:  {\color{blue}r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta}.
$$

When expressing our integral in cylindrical polar coordinates, we must write 

$$
{\color{blue}{\textrm{d}V}} = {\color{blue}r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta}.
$$

It's important not to forget the extra factor of ${\color{blue}{r}}.$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{r}^{2}}{r}^{3}\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating this integral using the usual methods, we get

$$
\int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,white]{\color{black}1}} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,white]{\color{black}1 - r^2 }} \bbox[2pt,white]{\color{black} r^3} \: \mathrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta
=
\dfrac{\pi}{6}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R x^2 + y^2 \:\textrm{d}V = \dfrac{\pi}{6}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130470 :tutorial/content "Let's now build some intuition behind the meaning of the volume element $\textrm d V.$ This will help us to understand the change of variables formula in cylindrical polar coordinates. Imagine moving from $P$ to $Q$ as follows:

- First, we move a distance $\textrm d x$ parallel to the $x$-axis so that the new point $P'$ has the same $x$-coordinate as $Q.$

- Then, we move a distance $\textrm d y$ parallel to the $y$-axis so that the new point $P''$ has the same $y$-coordinate as $Q.$

- Finally, we move a distance $\textrm d z$ parallel to the $z$-axis to land to $Q.$

These movements span the rectangular solid shown above. The volume of this solid, denoted $\textrm d V,$ is given by

$$

$$

Thus, the element $\textrm d V$ represents the volume generated by moving from the point $P$ to the point $Q$ in this coordinate system." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130473 :tutorial/content "Let's now repeat this process for a cylindrical polar system. If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](images/e2/e289cfbd210112a619018a7b905f7f2b1a9859ecb84b2517dd745705624d79d7.png)

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $\sqrt{3}$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ and

- bounded above by $z=x+9=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +9.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le \sqrt{3},\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta <\frac{\pi }{2},\,r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \le z\le r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +9\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}(x-y)\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{\int }_{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }^{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +9}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )[z]_{z=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }^{z=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +9}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +9-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}9{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}[3{r}^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )]_{r=0}^{r=\sqrt{3}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}3(\sqrt{3})^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}9\sqrt{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =9\sqrt{3}[\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{\theta =-\pi /2}^{\theta =\pi /2} \\  & =9\sqrt{3}(1-(-1))+9\sqrt{3}(0-0) \\  & =18\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-8382ccc3-43fb-56df-8da1-731b85bcec1a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-13092669-e4dd-5fb1-923f-23241a6ac139" :answer-field/id #uuid For example, suppose we want to evaluate the triple integral

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R x^2 + y^2 \:\textrm{d}V
$$

where $R$ is the finite region enclosed between the surfaces $z =0$ and $z = 1 - x^2 - y^2,$ as shown below.

![](images/a6/a63e349d2776fe07077379b9d603e32ad2ff264cfa8005a226422b44f7e100fe.png)

 

This is a challenging integral to evaluate as it currently stands. However, we should recognize that the problem naturally lends itself to cylindrical polar coordinates.

Recall that if $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad
y = r\sin\theta, \qquad 
z = z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](images/b2/b2f8a6fe7f21b062eec294522e411c1e471b564eae68763d4767f917d65b54b0.png)

Notice that the region $R$ is

- bounded below by $z = 0,$ and

- bounded above by $z = 1 - x^2 - y^2 = 1 - r^2.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi, \: 0 \leq z \leq 1-r^2 \right\}.
$$

![](images/da/dae76df462a695e655ffdde01559d19bf245aa6d601100fb8c7bc1024106a4c8.png)

 

To express our integral in terms of cylindrical polar coordinates, we will use the change of variables formula, given by

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, {\color{blue}\mathrm{d}V} = 
\iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \:  {\color{blue}r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta}.
$$

When expressing our integral in cylindrical polar coordinates, we must write 

$$
{\color{blue}{\textrm{d}V}} = {\color{blue}r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta}.
$$

It's important not to forget the extra factor of ${\color{blue}{r}}.$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{r}^{2}}{r}^{3}\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating this integral using the usual methods, we get

$$
\int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,white]{\color{black}1}} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,white]{\color{black}1 - r^2 }} \bbox[2pt,white]{\color{black} r^3} \: \mathrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta
=
\dfrac{\pi}{6}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R x^2 + y^2 \:\textrm{d}V = \dfrac{\pi}{6}.
$$"] [17592186130470 :tutorial/content "Let's now build some intuition behind the meaning of the volume element $\textrm d V.$ This will help us to understand the change of variables formula in cylindrical polar coordinates. We start by considering the usual rectangular coordinate system.

- bounded above by $z = 4 - y = 4 - r\sin{\theta}.$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the cylinder $x^2+y^2=5$ for $x\geq 0,$ $y\geq 0$ and between the surfaces $z=y$ and $z=y+3.$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$

y = r\sin\theta, \qquad 
z = z.

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](images/b7/b7b37ffe8e97ed4a661ee98750894641c6ed3354864dd5b54d2ed076e4fdb69b.png)

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $\sqrt{5}$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=y=r\sin\theta,$ and

- bounded above by $z=y+3=r\sin\theta + 3.$

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq \sqrt{5}, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \: r\sin\theta \leq z \leq r\sin\theta + 3\right\}.

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}x+2y\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{5}}{\int }_{r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }^{r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{5}}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )[z]_{z=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }^{z=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{5}}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{5}}3{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[{r}^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )]_{r=0}^{r=\sqrt{5}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{(\sqrt{5})}^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}5\sqrt{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =5\sqrt{5}[\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =\pi /2} \\  & =5\sqrt{5}(1-0)-10\sqrt{5}(0-1) \\  & =15\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}

For example, suppose we want to evaluate the triple integral

$$\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R x^2 + y^2 \:\textrm{d}V$$

where $R$ is the finite region enclosed between the surfaces $z =0$ and $z = 1 - x^2 - y^2,$ as shown below.

![](images/a6/a63e349d2776fe07077379b9d603e32ad2ff264cfa8005a226422b44f7e100fe.png)

This is a challenging integral to evaluate as it currently stands. However, we should recognize that the problem naturally lends itself to cylindrical polar coordinates.

Recall that if $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta, \qquad z = z.$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](images/b2/b2f8a6fe7f21b062eec294522e411c1e471b564eae68763d4767f917d65b54b0.png)

Notice that the region $R$ is

- bounded below by $z = 0,$ and
- bounded above by $z = 1 - x^2 - y^2 = 1 - r^2.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

$$\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi, \: 0 \leq z \leq 1-r^2 \right\}.$$

![](images/da/dae76df462a695e655ffdde01559d19bf245aa6d601100fb8c7bc1024106a4c8.png)

To express our integral in terms of cylindrical polar coordinates, we will use the change of variables formula, given by

$$\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, {\color{blue}\mathrm{d}V} = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \: {\color{blue}r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta}.$$

When expressing our integral in cylindrical polar coordinates, we must write $${\color{blue}{\textrm{d}V}} = {\color{blue}r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta}.$$ It's important not to forget the extra factor of ${\color{blue}{r}}.$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}((r\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2})\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta \\ & ={∭}_{Δ}{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}\theta +{sin}^{2}\theta )\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{r}^{2}}{r}^{3}\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}$$

Evaluating this integral using the usual methods, we get

$$\int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,white]{\color{black}1}} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,white]{\color{black}1 - r^2 }} \bbox[2pt,white]{\color{black} r^3} \: \mathrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R x^2 + y^2 \:\textrm{d}V = \dfrac{\pi}{6}.$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c6d9a5c4-532b-53e1-9689-7b5dbc30ec98" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7193 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} $$x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta, \qquad z = z.$$

- bounded below by $z = 0,$ and
- bounded above by $z = 1 - x^2 - y^2 = 1 - r^2.$
